questions.q: A project has "target": "ES2020" and calls orders.at(-1) (added in ES2022). What happens?
questions.explain: target rewrites syntax; it never adds functions. What TypeScript believes exists comes from lib, which defaults to the target's version. Raise the target, or add a newer lib if the runtime really has the function.
options: tsc rewrites at into older code that works everywhere
tsc reports that at does not exist, because with no lib setting the built-in types follow the target
It compiles, and crashes only on old runtimes
tsc adds a polyfill for at automatically

questions.q: A Node.js backend's tsconfig has no lib line. A developer writes localStorage.getItem("cart") in server code. What happens?
questions.explain: Without an explicit lib, TypeScript assumes a browser may be involved and includes the DOM types. A backend should write "lib": ["ES2024"] so browser APIs are compile errors.
options: It compiles, because the default lib includes DOM, and throws a ReferenceError when the server runs it
tsc replaces it with a file-based store

questions.q: In TypeScript 7, a fresh project with @types/node installed reports "Cannot find name 'process'". Why?
questions.explain: Older versions loaded every package in node_modules/@types. TypeScript 7 loads only the ones you name, which also keeps test-framework globals out of application code.
options: types defaults to an empty list, so no @types package is loaded until you list it: "types": ["node"]

questions.q: Under "module": "NodeNext", what decides whether a .ts file is emitted as an ES module or as CommonJS?
questions.explain: NodeNext mirrors Node.js: "type": "module" makes .js files ESM, otherwise CommonJS. That is why the same source produced import in one project and require in the other.
options: The file name must end in .esm.ts
The "type" field in the nearest package.json (or the .mts/.cts extension), exactly as Node.js decides at runtime

questions.q: A project with "type": "commonjs" and verbatimModuleSyntax uses import/export in its .ts files. What does tsc say?
questions.explain: verbatimModuleSyntax promises that imports are emitted exactly as written. Turning import into require would break that promise, so tsc refuses (errors such as TS1287 and TS1295). Use ESM, or write import x = require() in CommonJS.
options: Nothing; it converts them to require
It reports errors: ESM syntax cannot be written in a CommonJS file under verbatimModuleSyntax, because the output would not be "as written"
It switches the project to ESM

questions.q: Which module settings fit a React app built by Vite, where imports are written without extensions?
questions.explain: The bundler resolves and emits the code, so TypeScript should resolve like a bundler (extensionless imports allowed) and leave imports as written. NodeNext would demand .js extensions that the bundler does not need.
options: No module settings; Vite ignores tsconfig

questions.q: Which of these is not turned on by "strict": true?
questions.explain: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is separate, because it reports many errors in existing code. Turn it on yourself for new projects.

questions.q: What does strictNullChecks change about orders.find(...)?
questions.explain: The runtime behaviour does not change: find always could return undefined. The flag makes the type say so, so the compiler can make you handle it.
options: It makes find throw when nothing matches
Its type becomes Order | undefined, so using the result without handling "not found" is a compile error

questions.q: tsc reports "Property 'balanceKobo' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor." What is the best fix when the wallet starts empty?
questions.explain: Give the field its real starting value. The ! form only tells the compiler to trust you; at runtime the field would still be undefined, and += would give NaN.

questions.q: Why does useUnknownInCatchVariables make the catch variable unknown instead of any?
questions.explain: throw "timeout" is legal JavaScript. With any, error.message compiles and is undefined at runtime; with unknown, you write error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error).
options: Anything can be thrown (strings, numbers, objects), so you must check what it is before reading .message
To stop you from catching errors

questions.q: How do you fix "'this' implicitly has type 'any'" in function describeWallet() { return this.owner; } while keeping it a plain function?
questions.explain: The this parameter is only a type annotation; it is erased from the JavaScript. Callers must then call it with a suitable this, for example describeWallet.call(wallet). An arrow function would take this from outside, which is not what you want here.
options: Declare the type as a fake first parameter: function describeWallet(this: { owner: string })
Turn it into an arrow function

questions.q: strictFunctionTypes rejects assigning (p: CardPayment) => void to (p: Payment) => void. Why is that correct?
questions.explain: A function that needs more from its argument cannot stand in for one that accepts any payment. Parameters must be checked in the opposite direction from return values (contravariance).
options: Functions can never be assigned to each other
Callers of the second type may pass any payment, such as a bank transfer, and the card function would read a cardLast4 that is not there
CardPayment is a larger type, so it is always safe
Because arrow functions are not allowed as handlers

questions.q: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess on, which line still gives order the type Order (without | undefined)?
questions.explain: A for...of loop only visits items that exist. Index and record lookups can miss, so they get | undefined. That is exactly the distinction the flag makes.

questions.q: What does exactOptionalPropertyTypes change about phone?: string?
questions.explain: "Missing" and "present with the value undefined" behave differently: the second shows up in Object.keys and overwrites when spread. The flag keeps them apart unless the type says string | undefined.
options: The property may be missing, but may no longer be set to undefined explicitly
It removes the property at runtime

questions.q: With noImplicitOverride, a subclass writes override close(). Later the base class renames close to shutDown. What happens?
questions.explain: Without the keyword, the subclass method would silently stop overriding anything. With it, the rename becomes a compile error that points straight at the dead method.
options: The subclass method is renamed automatically
Nothing; the old method is just unused
tsc reports that close is marked override but the base class has no such member

questions.q: What is the difference between allowJs and checkJs?
questions.explain: With allowJs, a wrong call from TypeScript into a JavaScript file is caught. With checkJs, mistakes inside the JavaScript file are caught too, using inference and JSDoc comments.
options: They are two names for the same option
allowJs includes .js files in the program so TypeScript knows their exports; checkJs also reports type errors inside them

questions.q: A project has src/server.ts and test/server.test.ts, "outDir": "dist", and no rootDir or include. Where does server.js end up?
questions.explain: The default include picks up test/ too, so the computed root moves up one level. Set "rootDir": "src" and "include": ["src"].
options: dist/src/server.js, because the common folder of all inputs is the project root

questions.q: With "paths": { "@shop/*": ["./src/*"] }, the code passes tsc and runs under tsx, but node dist/main.js fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Why?
questions.explain: tsx and bundlers read paths themselves, which hides the problem during development. For Node.js, use package.json "imports" (keys starting with #), which both Node.js and NodeNext resolution understand.
options: tsc emitted the files in the wrong folder
paths only guides the type checker; tsc does not rewrite imports, so Node.js looks for an npm package called @shop/…
Node.js does not support ES modules

questions.q: Which alias works in both tsc (NodeNext) and plain node without extra tools?
questions.explain: Subpath imports are a Node.js feature, resolved at runtime. TypeScript's NodeNext resolution reads them too, and maps dist back to the sources while you edit.
options: A symlink in node_modules created by hand

questions.q: With sourceMap on, what does tsc add to each emitted .js file?
questions.explain: The comment is how Node.js (with --enable-source-maps) and browsers find the map, so that stack traces and breakpoints use your .ts lines.
options: The original TypeScript as a comment
A last line //# sourceMappingURL=file.js.map pointing at the map
Nothing; maps are only used by tsc

questions.q: A config extends a shared base and sets a few options on the command line. How do you see which options are really in effect?
questions.explain: --showConfig prints the final merged configuration, including options implied by others (such as isolatedModules from verbatimModuleSyntax), without compiling.

questions.q: The base config has "include": ["src", "test"]. The project config extends it and sets "include": ["src"]. What is included?
questions.explain: compilerOptions are merged option by option, but include, exclude and files are replaced entirely by the extending file.

questions.q: What does skipLibCheck skip?
questions.explain: Published declaration files were checked when they were built. Re-checking them is slow and can fail on conflicts between packages you cannot fix. Your own code is still fully checked.
options: Type checking of your own .ts files
Type checking of .d.ts declaration files, such as those in node_modules

questions.q: Under verbatimModuleSyntax, what is the difference between import type { AuditEvent } from "./audit.js" and import { type AuditEvent } from "./audit.js"?
questions.explain: import type marks the whole statement as type-only. A type modifier on one name marks only that name; the import statement itself is kept as written.
options: The first is removed completely; the second keeps an import {} from "./audit.js", so the module's side effects still run
The second is a syntax error
The first keeps the side effects, the second removes them

questions.q: A project uses verbatimModuleSyntax. What does TypeScript 7 emit for an exported const enum OrderStatus used in another file?
questions.explain: verbatimModuleSyntax implies isolatedModules and preserveConstEnums: each file must compile without reading others, so the value cannot be inlined across files. The const enum compiles like a normal enum.
options: Nothing: every use is replaced by the literal value
A normal enum object in its module, and normal property reads (OrderStatus.Paid) where it is used

questions.q: strict is already true by default in TypeScript 7. Why still write "strict": true?
questions.explain: An explicit line means the same thing to every tool and every version, and it documents the decision for the next reader.
options: Editors, linters and test tools may run an older TypeScript against the same file, and for them the default is false
The file is invalid without it
It enables extra flags that the default does not

questions.q: Turning on strictNullChecks in a large project reports 400 errors. Which approach is best?
questions.explain: Each error is a place where a missing value was not handled. Silencing them with ! or as keeps every bug and hides it. Fixing gradually, with a count that only goes down, keeps the project shippable meanwhile.
options: Keep the flag on, fix the errors directory by directory, and make CI fail if the count goes up

questions.q: How can a test make sure nobody quietly turns off noUncheckedIndexedAccess?
questions.explain: @ts-expect-error fails when there is no error on the next line. That turns "this flag is on" into something tsc checks on every run.
options: A small file with // @ts-expect-error above a line that only fails when the flag is on; if the flag is removed, the unused directive becomes an error

questions.q: Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, TypeScript types both values as number. What does this print?
questions.explain: Reading a missing index gives undefined at runtime whatever the type says, and undefined / 100 is NaN. noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds | undefined to both types so the compiler makes you handle it.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A property set to undefined exists, and spreading copies it over the stored phone. exactOptionalPropertyTypes would reject phone: undefined for a phone?: string property.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A missing property and one set to undefined read the same (undefined) but are different objects: in and Object.keys see the second one.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A thrown string arrives in catch as a string, and reading .message on a string gives undefined, not an error. This is why useUnknownInCatchVariables makes you check what you caught.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: The ! silences strictPropertyInitialization. What does this print?
questions.explain: The field starts as undefined, and undefined + 5000 is NaN. The definite assignment assertion told the compiler to trust you; it did not give the field a value.

questions.q: In plain JavaScript (no parameter checks), what does this print?
questions.explain: The second payment is a bank transfer with no card. This is the crash strictFunctionTypes prevents, by refusing to use a card-only function where any payment may arrive.

questions.q: In plain JavaScript, what does this print?
questions.explain: "5000" + 100 joins text. strictBindCallApply checks the arguments of call, apply and bind against the function's parameters, so the second call is a compile error in TypeScript.
options:
ada sends 5100
TypeError: amountKobo must be a number

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A finished iterator returns value: undefined. strictBuiltinIteratorReturn gives that result the type undefined instead of any, so calling a string method on it is a compile error.
options:
{ value: 'RICE-5', done: false }
{ value: undefined, done: true }

{ value: 'RICE-5', done: false }
{ value: 'RICE-5', done: true }

{ value: 'RICE-5', done: true }
{ value: undefined, done: true }

questions.q: Enums (and const enums under isolatedModules) exist at runtime as objects. What does this print?
questions.explain: A string enum compiles to an object whose keys are the member names and whose values are the strings. That object is what tsc emits for a const enum too when verbatimModuleSyntax is on.

questions.q: In an ES module (always strict mode), what does this print?
questions.explain: A plain call in strict mode gets this === undefined; a method call or call provides an object. noImplicitThis makes you declare what this must be, so the plain call becomes a compile error.

questions.q: Rewrite latestOrderTotal so it compiles under noUncheckedIndexedAccess and returns 0 for an empty list instead of crashing. Use at and an explicit check, no !.
questions.explain: at(-1) returns Order | undefined even without the flag. After the check, TypeScript narrows latest to Order, and the empty case has a defined answer.

questions.q: Write buildPatch(form) that returns a ProfilePatch containing only the fields whose value is not undefined, so it compiles under exactOptionalPropertyTypes and never erases stored data.
questions.explain: Leaving a field out, instead of setting it to undefined, is what "optional" should mean for a patch. The spread then only overwrites what the user actually changed.

questions.q: Write errorMessage(error: unknown): string: the message of an Error, the value itself for a string, and "Unknown error" for anything else.
questions.explain: With useUnknownInCatchVariables, error is unknown, and narrowing with instanceof and typeof is the only way to read from it. Every kind of thrown value gets a sensible message.
questions.expected:
Amount must be positive
gateway timeout
Unknown error

questions.q: Give describeWallet a this parameter so it compiles under noImplicitThis, then call it for Ada's wallet with call.
questions.explain: The this parameter is a type annotation only; it is erased. TypeScript now checks that every call provides a suitable this, and a plain describeWallet() becomes a compile error.

questions.q: Write priceLabel(prices, sku) that returns "SKU: ₦N" when the price exists and "SKU: not in catalogue" when it does not. It must compile under noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
questions.explain: A record lookup can miss, and the flag makes its type say so. Checking once narrows kobo to number for the rest of the function; without the check you would print ₦NaN.

questions.q: Finish SavingsAccount so it compiles under noImplicitOverride and strictPropertyInitialization: interestKobo starts at 0, and close() overrides the base method and adds the interest to the message.
questions.explain: interestKobo = 0 gives the field a real starting value, and override makes the replacement explicit. (The solution also writes the owner field out instead of using a parameter property, which keeps the code erasable for erasableSyntaxOnly.)

questions.q: Replace the const enum with an erasable alternative that works under verbatimModuleSyntax and erasableSyntaxOnly: an as const object OrderStatus and a type OrderStatus for its values.
questions.explain: An as const object is plain JavaScript plus erasable types, so every tool (tsc, tsx, Node type stripping) emits the same thing, and plain strings like "PENDING" are accepted. Enums compares the options in full.
questions.expected:
Paid, ready to ship Waiting for payment
[ 'PENDING', 'PAID' ]
